Weather that tells you what to do about it.
Used only to get the forecast where you are, rounded to about a kilometre.
Paper is warm white and amber. Vivid is cool white and azure, with brighter weather icons.
Two drawings of the same icons: solid shapes, or thin outlines.
The weather icons move: the sun turns, the rain falls, the lightning flashes.

No account, no ads, no tracking.
Units, appearance and update frequency go back to their defaults. Your places and your history are not affected.
The four screens, what the verdicts say, where the numbers come from

Chiaro tells you what the sky over your places is doing, and what to do about it: a sentence first, then the numbers that decided it. This guide walks through the four screens, says what each one answers, and points out the things worth knowing that a screen cannot say out loud.
The sky right now, and how the day will go.
The moments of the sky, and whether tonight is worth it.
What should tell you, and when.
How the forecast has been changing.
Your places are one tap away, behind the name at the top of the screen; the settings are behind the gear beside it.

The sky at the top is not a photograph: it is computed for this minute from the height of the sun, the clouds, the rain and the moon, so at three in the morning under a clear sky it is the same deep blue you would see outside. The thin band under it is the day itself, from first light to last, with the hour you are in marked on it.
When there is something worth saying — an umbrella around five, a thunderstorm at three — it is written above every number. When there is nothing to say, no sentence appears: quiet is an answer too.

Two places answer that: the sentence at the top and, right below it, the chances hour by hour, with the peak of the coming hours marked on the small rain curve. Chiaro describes rain the way its data arrives — how likely, how much, from when to when.

When what you are reading is no longer fresh, Chiaro says its real age instead of hiding it, and an update that failed says why. Pull the screen down to ask for a new one, or tap the age itself to try again.
An example: the age of what you are reading — tap it to try again.
Twenty-four hours of temperature, sky and rain chance, starting from the hour after this one: the hour you are in is the big number at the top.
One timeline for everything still ahead: sunrise or sunset, the golden and blue hours, the moment the sky goes fully dark, moonrise and moonset, and the hours rain is expected to start and ease off.
Seven days on one shared temperature scale, so the same bar length means the same thing on every row. The stripe under each day is its light, from dawn to dusk. Tap a day to open its hours.
UV, wind, humidity, dew point, pressure, visibility, air quality and pollen. Each number carries the line that says what to do about it, which is the only reason it is on the screen.
An example: two details, each with the line that says what to do about it.
When the latest update moves the days ahead, up to three sentences say how. Tap them and the whole story opens in the Journal.
Swipe sideways to move between your places; the dots under the sky say where you are. For a place that is not the one you are standing in, the header says what day and what hour it is there.

This is the screen no other weather app ships. It takes the moments worth waiting for — a sunrise, a golden hour, a night of stars, a meteor peak — and says whether tonight is one of the good ones. Everything on it is computed on your phone, so it works with no connection at all.
The card at the top is the dark window: the hours when the sky is genuinely dark and the moon is out of the way. It carries the verdict, the two hours it runs between, and the number that decided it.
A verdict is a word, a small sign and the number behind it — never a colour alone:
An example: a night of stars, judged by its clouds.

The number next to the word is the evidence that decided it, so you can weigh the answer yourself. When the forecast does not reach that far, or the last one that arrived is too old to trust, the answer is the honest one: a grey “not sure yet”, never a guess dressed up as a verdict.

The moments you follow, in the order they happen. One that is over is replaced by its next occurrence and the row says which day it is; one that is happening right now says so. It is the same moment the Sky widget shows on your home screen, resolved the same way.
An example: tomorrow\'s sunrise, judged by its clouds.

Each moment can remind you, with its own lead time or the usual one. Reminders are deliberately loose — they can arrive a few minutes early or late — and that looseness is exactly what keeps them off your battery. A reminder for something the clouds are going to hide stays quiet, unless you ask for it anyway.

The calendar ahead: meteor peaks with their dates, the next full moon, solstices and equinoxes — with a verdict where the forecast reaches that far and an honest “too far out to say” where it does not.

Some fifty moments, grouped by sun, night, moon, eclipses, seasons and meteor showers, each with the one line that says what it is and a page that explains it properly. This is the place to find out what a blue hour actually is, or the zodiacal light: by adding one, or by reading about it first.
Two kinds live here: the ones already written, and the ones you write. Nothing arrives that you did not switch on.

Three switches, each saying exactly what it sends and when: severe weather in the next 12 hours (at most one per storm), rain past 70% likely within 6 hours (at most twice a day), and the morning summary, once between 6 and 12.

Start from an idea — a window to run, ice tomorrow morning, a clear night — or build the sentence yourself: what to watch, how to compare it, the threshold, and a second condition if you want one. Values are picked, never typed, so an alert cannot be written wrong.
Runs your alert against the forecast already on the phone and tells you what it would have done. Nothing is sent, nothing is recorded.

Chiaro never rewrites it and never translates it. Words in braces become numbers when it fires: {trigger.value} is what set it off, {trigger.time} is when. Anything an alert can watch can be printed the same way, and the list under the message writes it for you.
Nothing extra: the checks ride the weather update you already asked for, at the rhythm you chose in the settings. Android asks for notification permission the first time you turn an alert on.
Every update leaves a line. The Journal is that record read as prose, newest first, grouped by day.

How the forecast moved for the days ahead, which of your alerts fired and when, which sky moments were actually observed and with what verdict — and the updates that did not make it, with the reason. A failed update is an entry, not a silence. When a day is over, one more line closes it: what the rain was given at, and whether it rained.
How the week has been moving

One row per day ahead, one column per six hours, the colour on the metric\'s own scale: rain, or the highs. A slot no update landed in stays empty, so a night with the phone off looks like the gap it was. A day whose forecast minimum is at or below zero carries a mark beside its name, with those days named underneath: freezing is a threshold, not a drift, so it gets a mark and a sentence rather than a scale of its own. It answers the question anyone planning a weekend actually asks — is this getting better or worse? Tap it to see the numbers behind the colours.
An example: three days, six slots, on the rain scale.
The name at the top of Today and Sky opens the list of places, and that is where they are all managed.
Type a couple of letters and the results arrive as you go; the searches you have already made stay within reach. Search needs a connection, everything else does not.

Optional, and only ever asked for when you turn it on. Chiaro takes the approximate position Android provides, rounds it to about a kilometre and sends that to Open-Meteo, which is the only way to ask for the forecast where you are; the name of the place comes from Android\'s own geocoder. Nothing is kept anywhere else, there is no account and no tracking, and the position is never read while the app is closed.
Move a place up or down and the swipe on Today follows that order. Swipe a place away to remove it, with a moment to undo if it was a mistake.

Now: icon, temperature, place — and on a wide or a tall card the day\'s sentence, or the sky\'s state when there is nothing to warn about; resize it and it shows what fits. Today: that, plus the whole sentence and the next hours. Sky: the moment in front of you and its verdict — the same one the Sky screen shows.

Press and hold a widget to open its own settings: which place it watches (the active one, or a fixed place of its own), its background — including the same computed sky the app draws — how solid that background is, and which weather icons it draws with.
Old data says how old it is, a widget with no place says so, and none of them shows a number it does not have. They repaint when an update lands, so they cost no battery of their own.

Units for temperature and wind. Appearance, where the theme, the palette, the two drawings of the weather icons and the wallpaper colors live. How often to look for a new forecast. The app language, on Android\'s own picker. Restoring the defaults puts units, appearance and frequency back as they started and leaves your places and your history exactly where they are.
Forecasts, air quality and place search come from Open-Meteo, an open weather service: free, no account, no API key. The weather request is the only thing that leaves your phone.
Sunrise, sunset, the moon and the whole sky module are computed right on your phone. That is why they are correct even with no connection at all.

When an update cannot get through, nothing goes blank: Chiaro keeps the last forecast that arrived, tells you how old it is, and quietly sets aside the hours that have already passed. What you see is always something the data really said.
Two minutes on where the numbers are born and how to read them.

A heads-up shortly before the sky moments you follow
A page each: what it is, when it happens, what it needs

Everything the app can follow above your place, with a page for each. This is where the words come from: what a blue hour is, why the earliest sunset is not the shortest day, what has to be true before the Milky Way is worth the drive.\n\nNone of it needs the network. The whole calendar is worked out from a latitude, a longitude and a date, so these pages and the times beside them still hold with the phone offline.
It happens once a day, and the app works out the time for the place you are watching.
It happens once a year, and the app works out the date for the place you are watching.
It has no fixed rhythm: the app looks with every update and says so when one is coming.
It is a single moment rather than a stretch of time.
It is a window, with a beginning and an end.
It is a matter of geometry rather than a sight, so it never carries a verdict: there is nothing here for the clouds to spoil.
Clouds decide whether it is worth your attention, so it carries a verdict read off the forecast.
It also needs a properly dark sky, so the moon and the twilight are part of the answer.

The moment the upper edge of the sun\'s disc touches the horizon. Not the centre: the almanac definition is the upper limb, and it includes the bend the atmosphere puts in the light. That bend is worth about half a degree, which is roughly the width of the sun itself, so when you see the sun appear it is in fact still geometrically below the horizon.\n\nThe time depends on your latitude and on the day of the year, and it moves fastest around the equinoxes: near 45° north, sunrise can shift by a minute and a half from one day to the next in late March, and barely a few seconds a day around the solstices.
The sun drops below the horizon.

The mirror of sunrise: the upper edge of the disc touching the horizon on the way down. Same half-degree of atmospheric refraction, so the sun you watch touch the sea has, strictly speaking, already set.\n\nSunset is the anchor of the evening for almost everything else in this guide. The golden hour ends near it, the blue hour follows it, civil twilight runs from it, and the night\'s darkness is counted from how far below the horizon the sun has gone since.
The sun at its highest point of the day.

The instant the sun crosses the local meridian — the highest point it will reach today, and the moment a shadow points due north or due south and is at its shortest.\n\nIt is almost never 12:00 on the clock, and the gap has two causes that stack. One is longitude: clock time is shared across a whole time zone, so a place at the eastern edge of one sees noon much earlier than a place at the western edge. The other is the equation of time, the wobble caused by the Earth\'s tilted axis and its elliptical orbit, which swings solar noon by up to a quarter of an hour either way over the year. Add summer time and the gap can pass ninety minutes.
Light enough to get around without streetlights, up to sunrise.

Civil twilight is the stretch with the sun between 6° below the horizon and the horizon itself. Morning civil twilight is that stretch before sunrise: it begins in a sky already clearly blue, and there is enough light to read outside and to see the landscape without a lamp.\n\nIt is the definition most laws use for lighting-up time, and it is when the last of the bright planets and Sirius are still visible against a brightening sky. At 45° north it lasts a little over half an hour at the equinoxes and close to three quarters of an hour in midsummer.
From sunset to when the streetlights earn their keep.

The evening half: the sun is below the horizon but not yet 6° below it. Light is fading fast but the landscape still has shape and colour, and you can still work outside without a lamp.\n\nIt ends at the moment most people would call \"night\", and its end is the beginning of the blue hour proper. The brightest stars come out during it, roughly in order of magnitude, which is why it is the most pleasant twilight to sit through.
The horizon line appears while the sky is still dark.

The sun between 12° and 6° below the horizon, before dawn. The name is literal: this is the window in which a navigator can still make out the sea horizon as a line while enough stars are visible to shoot with a sextant. Both at once, which is what makes it a useful category and not just a number.\n\nTo the eye it is the moment the sky stops being black and starts being deep blue in the east, well before anything you would call daylight. Landscape shapes are silhouettes, not objects.
The horizon fades out and the real evening begins.

The evening half: from 6° to 12° below the horizon. The sea horizon is still readable as a line, the first constellations are complete, and the last colour leaves the western sky during it.\n\nFor a photographer it is the end of usable ambient light. For an observer it is the waiting room: the sky is dark enough for bright deep-sky objects but still too bright for anything faint.
The last truly dark sky before the day arrives.

The sun between 18° and 12° below the horizon, before dawn. Below 18° the sun contributes no measurable light to the sky at all, so this is the boundary between real night and the first hint of the day.\n\nIts start is the end of astronomical night, and that is the practical meaning: the deep-sky window is closing. To the naked eye nothing appears to happen — the sky looks black throughout — but a long exposure sees the gradient arrive long before you do.
From here on the sky is properly dark.

The evening half: from 12° to 18° below the horizon. When it ends, the sky is as dark as it is going to get tonight from the sun\'s point of view, and astronomical night begins.\n\nAbove roughly 48.5° of latitude there are weeks in summer when the sun never gets 18° down and this event simply does not happen — the sky never finishes darkening. This guide has a pair of entries for exactly those weeks.
The first stretch after sunrise: warm, low light, the photographer\'s.

The morning twin: the same low-sun light, running from around sunrise until the sun has climbed high enough for the colour to go out of it.\n\nThe light is physically the same as the evening\'s, but the air is usually not: a night of cooling settles dust and often leaves mist in the low ground, so morning golden light tends to be cleaner and cooler, with more haze in the valleys. The practical difference is that you have to be there before it starts, which is why it is one of the moments most worth a reminder.
The last light before sunset, warm and low.

The stretch in the evening when the sun is low enough that its light reaches you through a very long slice of atmosphere. The long path scatters away the blue and leaves the warm end of the spectrum, so everything is lit sideways, in orange, with shadows several times longer than their objects.\n\nIt is called an hour for convenience only. Its real length is a matter of latitude and season: near the equator the sun drops almost vertically and the golden hour can be twenty minutes, while at 60° north in June the sun grazes the horizon for hours and the whole evening is golden. The app works out the real window for your place and for today, not a fixed hour before sunset.
The deep blue of the sky just before sunrise.

The morning twin of the blue hour: the same ozone blue, this time draining away instead of arriving, in the last minutes before civil twilight brightens the sky.\n\nFor photographs of lit buildings it works exactly like the evening one, with one difference in its favour: street lights are still on and the streets are empty.
The deep blue of the sky just after sunset.

The short window after sunset when the sun is roughly 4° to 6° below the horizon and the sky turns a deep, saturated blue. The colour is not simply \"less sunlight\": it comes from ozone high in the atmosphere, which absorbs the orange and red out of the light still passing overhead and leaves the blue behind.\n\nIt is the window in which the sky and artificial lights are the same brightness, which is why every photograph of a city that looks like the city remembers itself was taken in it. It is genuinely short — twenty to forty minutes at mid latitudes — and it does not wait.
Truly dark with the moon down: the window for the stars.

The part of the night that is genuinely dark: astronomical night — the sun more than 18° down — with the moon below the horizon as well.\n\nIt is the one event here that is an intersection rather than a crossing, and it is the reason this part of the app exists. Any ephemeris site will tell you when the sun sets; what an observer actually plans around is the overlap of \"the sun is far enough down\" and \"the moon is not up\", because a gibbous moon washes out a faint galaxy just as thoroughly as twilight does. Some nights the window is the whole night, some nights it is ninety minutes, and some nights there is none at all.

The moment the upper edge of the moon clears the horizon, refraction included, exactly as for the sun.\n\nThe moon rises on average about fifty minutes later each day, because it moves roughly 13° eastward along its orbit while the sky turns. That single fact explains most of what people find confusing about it: why a full moon rises at sunset and a new moon is up all day with the sun, and why the moon is sometimes an evening object and sometimes a morning one.
The moon drops below the horizon.

The moon\'s upper edge touching the horizon on the way down, refraction included, exactly as for the sun. Like moonrise it slips later by roughly fifty minutes a day, so the moon spends part of the month setting in daylight and nobody notices it at all.\n\nFor anybody looking at faint things it is the more useful of the two: moonset is when the sky gets its contrast back. That is why this app computes the darkness window as the overlap of astronomical night and a moon that is down, rather than treating moonlight as somebody else\'s problem.
Which moon is out: the phase, and how much of it is lit.

Today\'s moon as a statement rather than an event: which phase it is in and how much of the disc is lit.\n\nThe illuminated fraction is not the same thing as the phase name, and the gap matters more than it sounds. A moon three days from full is already 90% lit and will ruin a night of deep-sky observing, even though \"gibbous\" sounds comfortably far from \"full\". The number is the honest version, which is why the app prints it.
The instant of the next quarter: new, first quarter, full, last.

The next change of principal phase, whichever of the four comes first: new, first quarter, full or last quarter.\n\nOne entry that tracks the cycle instead of four that each wait for their own turn. The cycle from one new moon to the next averages 29 days 12 hours and 44 minutes, but any individual one can run half a day either side of that, because the moon\'s orbit is an ellipse and it does not travel at a constant speed. The app computes the real instant rather than adding an average.
Day and night nearly equal: spring starts in the north, autumn in the south.

The instant the sun crosses the celestial equator going north. It is a moment, not a day: the Earth\'s axis is momentarily side-on to the sun, and from that point the northern hemisphere is tilted towards it.\n\nThe name promises equal day and night, and it very nearly lies. The two are actually equal a few days earlier, for the same two reasons sunrise is not what geometry says: the almanac measures the sun\'s upper edge rather than its centre, and refraction lifts the whole disc into view before it has really arrived. Both add daylight at both ends.
The longest day in the north, the shortest in the south.

The instant the sun reaches its northernmost point, standing highest at noon and giving the longest day of the year in the northern hemisphere. The word means \"sun stands still\": for several days around it the noon altitude barely changes, which is what makes the exact instant something you compute rather than notice.\n\nIt is not the hottest part of summer, and it is not the day of the latest sunset. The heat lags by weeks because land and sea take that long to warm up, and the latest sunset comes days earlier for reasons of orbital geometry — this guide has separate entries for those extremes, because they are separate facts.
Day and night nearly equal: autumn in the north, spring in the south.

The sun crossing the celestial equator again, this time going south. From here the nights are longer than the days in the northern hemisphere, and they keep getting longer until the winter solstice.\n\nFor anybody who looks at the sky it is the real start of the year: darkness arrives at a civilised hour again, and the summer\'s short nights are over. It is also when the ecliptic starts standing steeply out of the morning horizon, which is what opens the autumn season for the zodiacal light before dawn.
The longest night in the north, the shortest in the south.

The sun at its southernmost point: the shortest day and the lowest noon sun of the year in the northern hemisphere.\n\nIt is the longest night, which makes it the best night of the year for observing if the weather cooperates, and it is famously not the day of the earliest sunset. That comes about two weeks earlier. Sunset starts getting later while sunrise is still getting later too, so the day keeps shrinking at the morning end after it has stopped shrinking at the evening end.
The early-January shower, short and intense.

Early January, and one of the three strong showers of the year: up to about 110 meteors an hour under a perfect sky. The debris comes from 2003 EH1, an object that behaves like an asteroid and is almost certainly a burnt-out comet.\n\nThe catch is the peak, which is genuinely sharp — a matter of hours rather than the day or two the big summer showers give you. Miss the window and you get a handful. The radiant is in northern Boötes, in a corner of sky that no longer has a constellation: Quadrans Muralis was dropped when the modern boundaries were drawn, and the shower kept the name.
The late-April shower, among the oldest on record.

Late April, a modest shower of about 18 an hour, from comet C/1861 G1 Thatcher — a visitor on a 415-year orbit that will not be back until the 2270s.\n\nIts real distinction is age: Chinese records describe it in 687 BC, which makes it the oldest meteor shower humanity has written down. It also has a habit of occasional outbursts, with rates jumping several times over without much warning. The radiant is near Vega, which is high and convenient from northern latitudes.
The May shower, born of Halley\'s comet.

Early May, and the debris is Halley\'s: the Earth passes through the stream comet 1P/Halley has left along its orbit, and does so twice a year. This is the first of the two passes.\n\nThe particles hit the atmosphere at about 66 km/s, among the fastest of any shower, so the trails are quick and often leave a glowing persistent train behind them. It strongly favours the southern hemisphere, where rates reach 50 an hour; from mid-northern latitudes the radiant barely clears the horizon before dawn and you get perhaps a dozen, all of them long grazing trails.
The late-July shower, at its best from the southern hemisphere.

Late July, around 25 an hour, most likely from comet 96P/Machholz. A steady, unhurried shower with a broad peak that lasts several days rather than a night.\n\nThe meteors are fainter and slower than the Perseids, and the two streams overlap in early August: a good share of what people count as Perseids in the last days of July is actually this shower. Best after midnight, when the radiant in Aquarius is highest, and it favours southern latitudes.
The August shower, the famous one.

Mid August, about 100 an hour, from comet 109P/Swift-Tuttle — a body 26 km across on a 133-year orbit. The best-known shower in the northern hemisphere, and it earns it: a high radiant, warm nights, and a peak broad enough that the nights either side are still worth going out for.\n\nThe meteors are fast, around 59 km/s, and often bright enough to leave trains. The one thing that decides your year is the moon: a Perseid peak near new moon is the show everybody describes, and one near full moon cuts what you see by three quarters. That is exactly what the full-darkness window in this app is for.
The early-October shower, best just after dark.

Early October, from comet 21P/Giacobini-Zinner. In an ordinary year it produces almost nothing — a few an hour — and in an extraordinary one it has produced thousands: there were storms in 1933 and 1946, and strong outbursts in 2011 and 2018.\n\nIt is also the rare shower to watch in the EVENING rather than after midnight. The radiant in Draco is highest just after dark and sinks through the night, which is the opposite of almost everything else in this list. The meteors are slow, around 20 km/s, because the Earth meets the stream almost head to tail rather than head on.
The late-October shower, also from Halley\'s comet.

Late October, about 20 an hour, and the second of the year\'s two passes through Halley\'s debris — the same comet that gives us the Eta Aquariids in May.\n\nUnlike its May twin this one is well placed from the northern hemisphere: the radiant sits near Betelgeuse, so it climbs high after midnight. The meteors are fast and often leave persistent trains, and the peak is broad and rather flat, so a week either side of the date is still productive.
The November shower, fast and now and then surprising.

Mid November, from comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle. In most years it is a quiet shower of about 15 an hour; roughly every 33 years, when the comet has just come back through the inner solar system, it can become a storm.\n\nThose storms are the most spectacular thing in this entire guide. In 1833 observers described tens of thousands of meteors an hour, falling thickly enough that people woke their neighbours; 1966 produced something similar over North America, and 1999 and 2001 gave strong displays. The meteors arrive at 71 km/s, the fastest of any annual shower, because the Earth meets this stream head on.
The December shower, the richest of the year.

Mid December, about 150 an hour: the richest and most reliable shower of the year, better than the Perseids and much less famous, because watching it means standing outside in December.\n\nIt is also the odd one out. The parent is not a comet but 3200 Phaethon, a rocky object that passes closer to the sun than Mercury does. Its debris is denser than cometary dust, so Geminid meteors are slow, bright and often distinctly coloured — yellow, green, sometimes blue. The radiant near Castor is up almost all night from northern latitudes, so there is no need to wait for the small hours.
The solstice shower, small and northern-only.

Around the winter solstice, from comet 8P/Tuttle. About ten an hour, and the least watched shower of the year: it falls in the days before Christmas, in the coldest week, right after the Geminids have spoiled everybody.\n\nIt has one genuine advantage. The radiant is in Ursa Minor, next to the pole star, so it never sets from the northern hemisphere and the shower can be watched at any hour of the night. It has also produced a few unexpected outbursts of around a hundred an hour, most recently in years when the comet was near aphelion — which is the opposite of what you would expect.
The bright core of the Milky Way, high enough to see, inside the astronomical night: March to October here, low in the south.

The window in which the bright centre of our own galaxy, the part in Sagittarius and Scorpius, stands more than 10° above the horizon inside astronomical night.\n\nThe whole Milky Way is up all year, but its core is the part that looks like something: the dense star clouds and the dark dust lanes that photographs are made of. From mid-northern latitudes it is a season, roughly March to October, and it never rises usefully high from far north. Below about 10° you are looking through too much atmosphere and too much of everybody\'s light pollution for it to be worth the drive.
A faint cone of light standing over the sunset: sunlight on dust along the ecliptic, visible only on the nights the ecliptic stands steeply.

A faint cone of light standing up from where the sun set, an hour or so after the sky has gone properly dark. It is sunlight scattered by dust spread along the plane of the solar system — the same plane the planets travel in — so it always leans along the ecliptic.\n\nYou can only see it when the ecliptic stands up steeply from the horizon rather than lying along it, which in the northern hemisphere means evenings in late winter and spring. It also needs a genuinely dark site: from a town it is not faint, it is absent. The app flags the nights the geometry is right, which is the half of the problem an app can answer for you.
The same cone before dawn, the one they used to call the false dawn.

The same dust cone, seen before dawn instead: rising from where the sun is about to come up, in the last dark hour of the night.\n\nIn the northern hemisphere its season is the mirror of the evening one — autumn mornings, when the ecliptic stands steeply out of the eastern horizon. Old books call this one the false dawn, because it looks exactly like the start of twilight in the wrong place and an hour too early.
The moon between us and the sun: the darkest sky of the month.

The instant the moon passes between the Earth and the sun, sharing the same celestial longitude. Its lit side faces entirely away from us, so there is nothing to see: this is an event you subscribe to precisely because it is invisible.\n\nIt is the best night of the month for everything else. New moon means no moonlight all night, which is why star parties and dark-sky trips are planned around it. When the alignment is close enough in latitude as well, you get a solar eclipse instead of an ordinary new moon.
Half lit and growing, high in the sky at sunset.

The moon a quarter of the way round its cycle: exactly half the disc lit, the right half seen from the northern hemisphere. It rises around midday and sets around midnight, so it owns the first half of the night.\n\nCounter-intuitively it is the best moon to actually look at. At full moon the sun is behind you and the surface is flat and glaring; at first quarter the light comes in sideways along the terminator, the line between lit and dark, and every crater throws a shadow. Any small telescope shows more here than it does at full.
Fully lit, rising as the sun sets and up all night.

The instant the moon is opposite the sun in the sky and the whole visible disc is lit. It rises around sunset and sets around sunrise, so a full moon is up for essentially the whole night.\n\nThat is exactly why observers dislike it: a full moon puts up enough light to read by and erases everything faint from the sky. It is also the moment the disc is at its least interesting through a telescope, for the same reason a photograph taken with a flash is flat. If the alignment is close enough, the moon passes into the Earth\'s shadow and you get a lunar eclipse.
Half lit and shrinking, high in the sky at dawn.

Half the disc lit again, the other half this time, three quarters of the way round the cycle. It rises around midnight and sets around midday, so it owns the second half of the night and is still up in the morning sky.\n\nIts practical value is the mirror of the first quarter\'s: the first half of the night is moonless. For anybody who would rather observe in the evening than at three in the morning, the week after last quarter is the second-best window of the month.
The full moon of the year that passes nearest the earth: about a seventh wider than the farthest one.

The full moon of the year that falls nearest to perigee, the near end of the moon\'s elliptical orbit. It is the biggest and brightest full moon of the year — what the newspapers call a supermoon.\n\nThe difference is real but modest: about 14% wider and around 30% brighter than a full moon at the far end of the orbit, which is a lot in a photograph and almost nothing to the naked eye, because you have nothing to compare it against. The genuinely large moon everybody remembers seeing is the moon illusion — a low moon near the horizon looks huge for reasons that happen inside your head, not in the sky.
The moon crossing the earth\'s shadow. Safe to look at, and visible from wherever the moon is up.

The moon passing into the shadow the Earth casts. It only happens at full moon, and only when the full moon falls close enough to the line where the moon\'s tilted orbit crosses the plane of the Earth\'s — otherwise the moon passes above or below the shadow, which is what happens most months.\n\nThe colour is the good part. The Earth\'s shadow is not empty: sunlight bent through the ring of atmosphere around our planet reaches the moon, and that light has had its blue scattered out of it by every sunrise and sunset on Earth at once. So a totally eclipsed moon goes copper red. A lunar eclipse is visible to everybody on the night side of the Earth at the same time, needs no equipment and is completely safe to watch.
The moon passing in front of the sun. How much it covers depends on where you stand, and it is never safe to look without a proper filter.

The moon passing in front of the sun. It happens at new moon, under the same alignment condition as a lunar eclipse, and the coincidence that makes it spectacular is that the moon and the sun look almost exactly the same size from here — the sun is about 400 times wider and about 400 times further away.\n\nNEVER look at a partial solar eclipse without a proper solar filter, and a telescope or binoculars without one will do permanent damage in less than a second. Note also that the app answers for YOUR place: an eclipse that is total somewhere on Earth is usually partial or invisible where you are, because totality falls in a track only a hundred kilometres or so wide.
The near end of the orbit, in the first week of January: the northern winter has nothing to do with distance.

The point in the year when the Earth is closest to the sun — early January, about 147 million kilometres.\n\nIt is the fact that settles the most common misunderstanding about the seasons: the northern hemisphere has winter when the Earth is at its CLOSEST. Distance has almost nothing to do with it. The seasons come from the 23.4° tilt of the axis, which decides how steeply the light lands and how long the sun stays up. The distance does something small and real: the Earth moves fastest at perihelion, which is why northern winter is a few days shorter than northern summer.
The far end, in the first week of July.

The far end of the orbit: early July, about 152 million kilometres from the sun. Five million kilometres further out than in January, which is about 3%.\n\nThe sun is correspondingly about 7% fainter, and the northern hemisphere is having its summer anyway — the tilt wins by a wide margin. Because the Earth travels slowest here, this is also the sluggish half of the orbit, and it is one of the reasons the calendar\'s seasons are not all the same length.
Not the solstice: the sun sets at its earliest about a fortnight before it.

The day of the year the sun sets earliest — about two weeks BEFORE the winter solstice, not on it.\n\nThe cause is the equation of time. A solar day, measured noon to noon, is not exactly 24 hours: the Earth\'s tilt and its elliptical orbit make it run a little long or a little short through the year, and in early December it runs long. So solar noon drifts later on the clock day by day, dragging sunset later with it, fast enough to beat the shortening of the day itself. Sunrise keeps getting later for weeks afterwards, which is why the darkest evenings and the darkest mornings are not the same date.
And it rises at its latest about a week after the solstice.

The day of the year the sun rises latest — about two weeks AFTER the winter solstice, the mirror of the earliest sunset.\n\nSame cause, other end. Solar noon is still drifting later through early January, and by then the day has started growing again, but the morning end is still losing the race. This is the date the winter actually feels longest, and it is the one people notice, because it is a fortnight after everybody has been told the days are getting longer.
The night stops getting fully dark, which happens above about 48 degrees of latitude.

The first night of the year on which the sun never gets 18° below the horizon, so astronomical night never arrives and the sky never finishes darkening.\n\nIt happens above roughly 48.5° of latitude, which is further south than most people expect: Paris, Vienna and Vancouver all have white nights, and so does most of northern France. It is not the midnight sun — the sun does set — but a blue glow stays in the northern sky all night, and the faint half of this guide shuts down until autumn.

The first night the sun manages to get 18° down again, and real astronomical night comes back.\n\nFor an observer at these latitudes it is the date the season opens. The darkness window becomes a real window again, the Milky Way\'s core is still up in the evening for a few more weeks, and the Perseids are usually within reach of it.
Few, slow and bright: this one makes fireballs. Shares its night with the delta Aquariids.

Late July, and the rate is almost beside the point: five an hour is a poor shower on paper. What this one produces is fireballs — slow, bright, unmistakable, the kind that make people stop talking.\n\nThe parent is comet 169P/NEAT, and the stream is unusual in being young and not yet spread out; models suggest it will become a major shower a few centuries from now. It shows equally well from both hemispheres, and because the meteors are slow and bright it is one of the few showers a moonlit night does not entirely ruin.
A long, slow autumn stream: not many, often very bright.

Late October into early November, from comet 2P/Encke, whose stream is old, wide and spread along a great deal of the Earth\'s path.\n\nThe rate is low — about five an hour — and the peak is so broad it is barely a peak at all, which is why the shower is described by its character instead: slow, deep orange fireballs. The southern branch and the northern one overlap through the autumn, and their combined weeks are the reason early November is when newspapers print fireball photographs.
The second half of the Taurids, in November.

Mid November, the northern branch of the same 2P/Encke stream, with the same low rate and the same taste for slow fireballs.\n\nThe two branches exist because the stream is old enough for the planets to have split it: Jupiter\'s gravity has worked on it for thousands of years and pulled it into filaments the Earth now crosses separately. Some years the Earth passes through a denser knot of larger fragments and the fireball count jumps — those are the \"Taurid swarm\" years, and they come round roughly every seven.
